summary.text: 面 is interpreted as a face picture, with an eye inside an outline. It commonly means “face” and also has recorded senses such as “surface” and “side.” In simplified Chinese, it also writes the flour and noodle word written 麵 in traditional Chinese.

formation.text: Pictographic: the oracle graph has competing analyses. One reads it as an eye inside a face outline; another reads it as 目 within an outline, while the received Shuowen account relates 面 to 𦣻 and describes it as shaped like a human face. The ancient construction and graphic transitions remain disputed.

components.text: 面 is treated here as one pictorial graph. One analysis reads an eye within a face outline; another assigns the inner form to 目 and the outer form to a face outline. The received Shuowen account instead relates the graph to 𦣻; these analyses do not establish separate current components.

history.text: The cited scholarly account distinguishes oracle forms interpreted as 目 inside an outer face outline from Western Zhou bronze forms used only as a component and interpreted there as a head-related form with an indicator for the face. It describes the Chu-slip form as apparently developing from the Western Zhou shape, and later Qin, seal and early Han forms as combining developments from oracle and Western Zhou shapes. These interpretations do not establish a single graphic sequence.

The received Shuowen explanation relates 面 to 𦣻 and describes it as shaped like a human face. The cited paleographic accounts disagree about how this later head-related analysis relates to the oracle forms; 靣 is recorded as a variant, with no established ancestry linking it to 面.

In simplified Chinese, 面 is used where traditional Chinese writes 麵 for the flour and noodle word. The related graph 麪 is recorded as an older spelling and analyzed with 麥 for meaning and 丏 for sound. The exact transition to 麵 is unresolved; this spelling relationship does not show that the face word 面 gave rise to the food word.

uncertainties.text: The individual oracle inscriptions and their dates were not verified. Scholarly analyses disagree over the inner element and its relation to the later 𦣻/首 analysis; proposed graphic pathways remain unresolved. The report that 面 is absent from bronze inscriptions does not specify the surveyed corpus’s limits.
The dates and semantic links among the recorded uses “face toward,” “surface,” “side,” and “dimension” remain unresolved.
The evidence does not establish the exact chronology of 麪 and 麵, separate earliest attestations for flour and noodles, or phonetic borrowing of the food word from the face word.

senses.period: oracle-bone script period; individual attestations undated
senses.text: Paleographic accounts interpret oracle-period forms as depicting a face. This is a proposed reading of the graph; the individual inscriptions and their dates were not verified, so the evidence does not establish this as the earliest attested use.

senses.period: Chu-slip text cited by a modern database; date not supplied
senses.text: 面 is recorded with the sense “face toward” in a Chu-slip text.
Dictionary records list “surface,” “side,” and “dimension.” Their dates and links to the face and facing senses are unresolved.

senses.gloss: flour, dough, noodles (written 面 in simplified Chinese for 麵)
senses.text: In simplified Chinese, 面 writes the flour and noodle word for which traditional Chinese uses 麵. This is a writing substitution; the evidence does not establish semantic development from “face” or sound-based borrowing from the face word.

limitations.text: Dates and links among the facing, surface, side, and dimension uses remain unresolved; the cited facing use does not by itself establish a semantic development from “face.”

The relationship between 面 and 麵 as spellings is supported, but the exact chronology of 麪 and 麵 and the separate earliest attestations of flour and noodle senses remain unresolved. The evidence does not establish borrowing of the food word from the face word.

relationships.text: In simplified Chinese, 面 is the standardized counterpart of traditional 麵 in the flour and noodle word. This whole-character writing relationship does not make 麵 an internal component of 面 or establish borrowing from the face word.

components.text: Treat 面 as one face picture. Ancient analyses disagree about whether its inner shape represents an eye or the character 目.

items.period: Shuowen seal-script style; associated with the transmitted Shuowen tradition, not a dated artifact
items.caption: A modern vector drawing of 面 in seal-script style. The enclosing outline and inner shape are visible, though this redraw alone does not establish the graph’s historical interpretation.
items.alt: Black seal-script form of 面, with a broad outer enclosure around an inner shape.
items.selection_reason: Identifies the entry character in seal-script style; the face interpretation of earlier oracle forms is supported separately by paleographic analysis.

items.period: Shuowen seal-script style; the dictionary identifies 麪 as the Shuowen form and 麵 as a later common spelling
items.caption: A modern vector drawing of 麵 in seal-script style, visibly including 麥 on the left. Dictionary accounts identify 麪 as the Shuowen form, analyze it with 麥 for meaning and 丏 for sound, and record 麵 as a later common spelling.
items.alt: Black seal-script form of 麵, with 麥 on the left and a tall enclosed shape on the right.
items.selection_reason: Shows the 麥 component and helps explain the dictionary-recorded 麪 and 麵 spellings used for the flour and noodle word. The redraw itself does not establish a historical path between these forms or their relation to 面’s face history.

limitations.text: These are modern vector drawings in seal-script style, not images of dated artifacts. Their shapes do not establish chronology or the path between the recorded forms; 面’s oracle graph is interpreted as a face with an eye in paleographic analysis.
